title: The Mended Net
logline: A fishing crew's net comes back from the water cut clean through, torn by a rival boat working too close to their ground. Before it fishes again, it has to be mended, knot by knot, on the sand.

object.note: Object 3 (identity not chosen) could enter only if the crew genuinely offers or discards a torn or mended piece of gear. Never staged.

thread_in.thread: The catch that went to someone else becomes a net cut by someone else: blocked wanting starts to push back, and the heat of the next stage begins on another shore.

thread_out.thread: From a rival on the water to a threat that comes out of the dark: the question of what wanting turns into when something stands in the way follows a farmer up into a watch hut for the night.

requirements: A fishing community with a real, current or recent dispute over grounds or gear
A crew willing to show the damage and the repair, and to speak about the dispute on their own terms
Access that does not require naming or filming the other side without consent

suggestions.name: Fishing villages of the Jaffna peninsula coast
suggestions.why: A coastline with many small fishing communities and long-contested inshore grounds; well known as an active fishing region.
suggestions.verify: Confirm a specific community, a real current dispute, and willingness to be filmed discussing it.

lesson.in_simple_terms: Anger often starts as wanting: we want something, something gets in the way, and the wanting turns against whatever blocked it. The texts say this state always comes with pain, and the first person it hurts is the one who feels it.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: අප යමක් පතද්දී ඊට බාධාවක් ආ විට ඒ ආශාවම තරහක් බවට හැරෙන අතර, ඒ තරහේ වේදනාව මුලින්ම දැනෙන්නේ තරහ ගන්නා කෙනාටමයි.
lesson.the_teaching: The Abhidhamma counts two hate-rooted states of mind, and both always come with a painful mental feeling (domanassa) and with aversion (paṭigha), the mind 'striking against' what it dislikes. Pradeepika shows the turning point in an example: a person wants something, a living being stands in the way, and from the moment the wish becomes 'remove the obstacle' the state is no longer wanting but aversion. Among the ordinary occasions for it, the text names not getting what one wants.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The cut net is laid out and examined by hand, and the crew's first words on seeing it carry the turn from loss to heat. Through the long, patient mending, talk about the other boat flares and subsides, and the viewer can notice that the displeasure lives in the people on the sand, far from the rival boat. The film never rules on who was in the right.

key_terms.en: aversion, irritation; literally 'striking against' the object

lesson.caution: This does not mean anger becomes acceptable once it feels justified; the texts make no exception for 'righteous' anger, though they also pass no verdict on who was right in the crew's dispute.
lesson.builds_on: The previous stage ended with wanting that is blocked; this film shows the next step the texts describe, the moment blocked wanting turns against whatever stands in its way.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
